text: The DAWbench project was originally meant to test audio interface performance (they ran all interface tests on the same PC to compare device results), but if you flipped it around and tested different computers with the same interface/OS/drivers you can make it a test of the DAW PC rather than the interface. The "DAWbench VI 2023" is the best for this purpose (there's another "DSP" test which highlights the interface more). Link: https://dawbench.com/ But generally, when shopping, look for the highest single-core clock rate you can afford. While all modern DAWs support multi-core, individual tracks/channels are still generally hosted on a single thread, so you want fast cores for high performance/low latency for tracks with long plugin chains. I don't know much about AMD, but Intel recently has released CPUs with mixed "performance" and "efficiency" cores, so you will see 2 different clock rates listed. The performance cores are the true i5/i7/i9 ones, and the efficiency ones are low-power Atom cores. Different DAWs might handle this kind of situation in different ways as developers come to grips with this new development. (Again, I don't know if this is a consideration with AMD chips.) For Windows, just about any off-the-shelf laptop or desktop with i7 or above (or the AMD eqivalent) will be a fine DAW computer. But even some i5-level systems should work well for most users.

text: Small amounts of clipping at multiple stages. Clip your Snare track, clip your drum bus, clip your master. True peak limiter can help - many of us use FabFilter's Pro L2. Saturate low end instruments and lower the resulting harsh brightness with a high shelf. EQ out some of the muddy 250-500hz range. Check your low end with a spectrum analyzer and make tame any wild bass frequencies with a multiband compressor. That's all I got for now.

text: Make it sound good according to the style. Normalization only uses gain, you can do the same inside your DAW. Just import a reference and level match it to your mix. Compare the mix quality by ear. Also, stop obsessing about LUFS and trying to get the smallest (loudest) number. Take in consideration that normalization is done to integrated LUFS, but you still have momentary LUFS which tell you more about your dynamics (punch).
label: analysis

text: I use a compressor where you are using a limiter. The saturation before the clipper is already giving me the rms boost I need. The clipper keeping all the hits the same volume is what allows the compressor to shape each hit the same way. Even if you're using real drums instead of samples.
